summary: Specifies an enhanced version of Mobile IPv6 route optimization. It aims for lower handoff delays, stronger security, and less signaling overhead than the original procedure. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: When you move, your mail normally goes to your old house first and then gets forwarded. This makes the trip shorter and safer, so mail finds you faster.

subtitle: Faster, more secure mobile node route optimization using cryptographic address binding.

tldr.problem: Base Mobile IPv6 route optimization has slow handoff delays because both home and care-of addresses must be verified through exchange of messages, and it is vulnerable to attackers on the path between the mobile node and home agent.
tldr.mechanism: Uses cryptographically generated home addresses (CGAs) to prove ownership without a public-key infrastructure, allows concurrent care-of address verification while sending data, and limits redirection-based flooding attacks through credit-based authorization.
tldr.outcome: Achieves lower handoff latency, stronger security against path attackers, reduced signaling overhead, and longer binding lifetimes compared to base Mobile IPv6.

facts.label: Binding refresh period
facts.value: Can extend beyond 7 minutes when using CGA

today: RFC 4866 is a Standards Track specification that provides enhanced security and performance for Mobile IPv6. It remains the authoritative definition of route optimization enhancements using cryptographically generated addresses and concurrent care-of address verification, widely implemented in production mobile IPv6 deployments.

sections.title: The Challenge of Securing Mobile Connections
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6, defined in RFC 3775, allows a mobile node to maintain connectivity using a stable home address even as it moves between networks. When away from home, the mobile node registers its current network attachment (its care-of address) with a correspondent node. The correspondent node then redirects packets destined for the home address to the care-of address, enabling direct communication without routing through the home agent.

However, base Mobile IPv6 faces three significant challenges. First, when a mobile node moves to a new network, it must verify both its home address and its new care-of address to the correspondent node through a process called the return routability procedure. This verification requires multiple message exchanges, creating handoff delays that affect interactive applications, real-time services, and TCP throughput.

Second, the return routability procedure is vulnerable to attackers positioned on the path between the correspondent node and the victim. Such attackers can intercept verification messages and redirect bindings.

Third, repeated binding refreshes and address verification consume signaling bandwidth. Mobile IPv6 requires correspondent registrations to be refreshed every 7 minutes even without movement, consuming roughly 7 bits per second of traffic for a mobile node communicating with a stationary peer.
sections.eli5: When you move, you have to prove to everyone who talks to you where you are now. This proof takes time and can be tricked by someone listening to your messages. It also creates a lot of proof messages even when you are standing still.

sections.title: Three Design Goals
sections.content:
Enhanced Route Optimization addresses three specific objectives. Handoff latency reduction aims to eliminate the delay imposed by address verification. In base Mobile IPv6, a typical handoff delay includes a round-trip time to the home agent for home registration, an additional round-trip time to the home agent plus a round-trip to the correspondent node for the return routability procedure, and a one-way time for the Binding Update message to propagate. Enhanced Route Optimization targets elimination or reduction of these delays.

Security strengthening protects against both attackers off the path and, to the degree possible, attackers positioned on the path. While a correspondent registration must still prevent impersonation, denial-of-service, and redirection-based flooding (amplified DDoS attacks), the goal is security comparable to non-mobile Internet communications.

Signaling overhead reduction aims to lower the bandwidth consumed by binding refreshes and verification, particularly for mobile nodes that move infrequently or not at all. A mobile node that moves once every 30 minutes generates roughly 1.7 bits/s of signaling traffic, but a high-mobility scenario at 120 km/h in a 100-meter cell creates about 1,000 bits/s of overhead, comparable to compressed voice traffic.
sections.eli5: The design wants three things: faster proof exchanges when you move, stronger math-based proof that is harder to trick, and fewer refresh messages when you stay in one place.

sections.title: Core Design Mechanisms
sections.content:
Enhanced Route Optimization combines several techniques. Cryptographically Generated Addresses (CGAs) bind a home address to a public key such that any node can verify the binding without infrastructure. A node that generates a CGA proves ownership by demonstrating knowledge of the corresponding private key. This eliminates repeated home address tests after an initial verification; subsequent binding updates simply prove knowledge of the private key through a signature.

Non-cryptographic care-of addresses remain simple because a care-of address identifies a location, not an endpoint. Instead of cryptographic proof, the protocol verifies reachability through a lightweight test.

Concurrent care-of address tests allow a correspondent node to begin sending data to a tentative care-of address (in UNVERIFIED state) while verification proceeds. The mobile node can resume bidirectional communication immediately after a handoff, without waiting for address proof.

Semi-permanent security associations cache authentication state. After the initial CGA-based authentication, mobile and correspondent nodes exchange a shared secret token called a permanent home keygen token. Subsequent bindings use this token instead of expensive public-key operations, reducing computational cost and message size.

Credit-based authorization prevents redirection-based flooding attacks that exploit concurrent unverified care-of addresses. A correspondent node tracks 'credit' earned through receiving data from a verified address, and spends this credit by sending data to an unverified address. Once credit is depleted, the correspondent node either discards outbound data or sends it via the home agent, limiting amplification attacks to the level of direct flooding.

Parallel home and correspondent registrations allow a mobile node to simultaneously initiate both registrations, reducing total handoff delay.
sections.eli5: The design uses math (CGA) to prove identity once, then caches that proof. For the new address, it lets the post office start delivering right away without waiting for proof. It also uses a 'credit' system to stop flood attacks: you earn credit by sending mail, and the post office can only forward a limited amount of our mail to your new address until the address is fully verified.

sections.title: Binding Update Message Flow
sections.content:
When a mobile node moves to a new network, it sends a Binding Update message to the correspondent node. The message may be sent in two forms. An early Binding Update is sent immediately with a zero care-of keygen token, allowing the correspondent node to register the new care-of address in UNVERIFIED state and begin receiving data. A complete Binding Update follows once the mobile node obtains a valid care-of keygen token, moving the address to VERIFIED state.

The Binding Update is authenticated using one of three methods, depending on whether the mobile node's home address is a CGA and whether a permanent home keygen token is cached. If the home address is a CGA and no token is cached, the mobile node proves knowledge of its private key by including its CGA parameters and a signature in the Binding Update. If a permanent home keygen token exists, the mobile node proves knowledge of this shared secret instead, avoiding expensive CGA operations. If the home address is not a CGA, the mobile node falls back to traditional home address reachability proof.

When the correspondent node receives a Binding Update, it validates the authenticator according to the chosen method, registers the binding, and returns a Binding Acknowledgment message. If the Binding Update included CGA parameters and was authenticated via CGA, the correspondent node responds with a fresh permanent home keygen token (encrypted with the mobile node's public key). If the Binding Update was early, the correspondent node includes a care-of keygen token for use in the complete Binding Update message.
sections.eli5: The mobile node says 'I moved, here is my new address, and here is math proof I am really me.' The correspondent node checks the proof and says 'Okay, I will start sending to your new address, but I will only send as much as you have earned credit for until you prove the address is actually yours.'

sections.title: Credit-Based Flooding Prevention
sections.content:
The correspondent node maintains a credit counter for each mobile node. When a payload packet arrives from a care-of address in VERIFIED state, the correspondent node increases the credit counter by the size of the received packet. This earned credit is then available for sending data to an UNVERIFIED care-of address.

When sending outbound payload packets, the correspondent node checks the care-of address state. If VERIFIED, it sends normally. If UNVERIFIED and the credit counter equals or exceeds the packet size, it sends the packet and decreases the counter. If UNVERIFIED and credit is insufficient, it either discards the packet or buffers it, preventing amplified attacks.

Credit aging prevents a malicious node from slowly building credit over a long period and then flooding a victim in a burst. The correspondent node periodically multiplies all credit counters by a factor less than one (e.g., 0.875 every second), ensuring an upper bound on the flooding rate when an address is unverified.
sections.eli5: Think of it like a gift card: you earn credit by sending messages, and you can use that credit to have messages sent to your new address while it is being verified. The card balance slowly decreases over time, so you cannot save up a huge amount and then spend it all on flooding.

sections.title: Security Analysis
sections.content:
Enhanced Route Optimization provides multiple security improvements. Home address ownership is protected through a CGA that cryptographically binds the home address to a public key. A signature over the Binding Update message proves knowledge of the private key, and this proof is valid for the lifetime of the CGA without repeated verification, provided the home address prefix has been validated once.

An initial home address test remains necessary to prevent attacks where a malicious node generates a CGA with a spoofed home address prefix and requests redirection of traffic to a victim. The initial test occurs proactively before handoff when possible, avoiding delay during the critical handoff period.

Care-of address ownership is established through reachability proof: if a node can receive at an address, it owns that address. Unverified care-of addresses are protected against amplified redirection-based flooding through credit-based authorization.

Protection against on-path attackers is achieved through CGA signatures. An attacker on the path between correspondent and mobile nodes cannot downgrade the authentication method from CGA-based to reachability-based proof, because a Binding Update authenticated via CGA must include a non-null home nonce index. Once a permanent home keygen token is established via CGA authentication, subsequent updates use the token, which an on-path attacker cannot forge without the shared secret.

The RFC explicitly notes that Enhanced Route Optimization achieves a security level comparable to non-mobile Internet communications, satisfying security requirements at the IPv4 equivalent level. Applications requiring higher security should use IPsec or TLS.
sections.eli5: You prove you are really you by signing messages with your private key. The post office can trust that signing. Once they trust you, you can use a simpler proof (the shared token) for future moves. If someone on the path tries to trick the post office, the signature stops them from downgrading to the simpler proof.

sections.title: New Mobility Options
sections.content:
Enhanced Route Optimization introduces several new mobility options carried in Binding Update and Binding Acknowledgment messages. The CGA Parameters option carries the mobile node's CGA parameters, which may span multiple options because each option is limited to 255 bytes. Multiple CGA Parameters options are always directly followed by a Signature option.

The Signature option contains a signature over the Binding Update message using the mobile node's private key. The signature is calculated over the care-of address, correspondent node address, and the Binding Update content.

The Permanent Home Keygen Token option is included by the correspondent node in a Binding Acknowledgment message to provide a shared authentication secret. The token is encrypted using the mobile node's public key with RSAES-PKCS1-v1_5 format.

The Care-of Test Init option in an early Binding Update requests the correspondent node to generate and return a care-of keygen token for use in a subsequent complete Binding Update. The Care-of Test option in the Binding Acknowledgment returns this token.

The CGA Parameters Request option in a Binding Update asks the correspondent node (if its IP address is a CGA) to prove ownership of its address by including CGA parameters and signature in the Binding Acknowledgment.

A new set of status codes provides feedback: 147 indicates no permanent home keygen token is available, 148 indicates CGA verification failed, 149 indicates a permanent token already exists, and 150 indicates a non-null home nonce index was expected.
sections.eli5: The protocol carries several new pieces of information in messages: the math proof (signature), the shared secret token, requests for tokens, and response codes that explain why something did not work.
